description: We are a motivated team passionate about space exploration, Earth science, software, and data analysis. We enjoy working with open data and turning ideas into practical solutions. For this challenge, we aim to compare Earth environments with the Moon and Mars and identify potential analog sites. Join us if you enjoy solving problems, brainstorming, and building prototypes. We value curiosity, teamwork and communication
summary:
Landing near the Moon’s south pole is challenging due to uneven terrain, extreme lighting conditions, and limited direct communication with Earth. Our project addresses these challenges by combining real NASA data with artificial intelligence and scientific analysis.

Using NASA JPL Horizons and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) topographic data, our system analyzes solar illumination, Earth visibility, and the influence of lunar terrain on potential landing sites. An AI-powered computer vision module identifies surface hazards, such as craters and rocks, to support the selection of safer landing zones.

We also developed a physical lunar surface prototype to demonstrate how the system can analyze terrain before landing.

SafeLanding AI helps transform complex space data into practical mission-planning insights, supporting better landing-site selection, more reliable communication planning, and future autonomous lunar exploration.
details:
How does it work?

Our project addresses two major challenges of lunar landing missions: choosing suitable landing locations and identifying hazards during descent.

The Mission Planner analyzes the positions of the Sun and Earth using NASA JPL Horizons astronomical data. It helps evaluate solar illumination and direct Earth visibility, both of which are essential for power generation, communication, and mission planning.

To improve accuracy, we integrated NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) topographic data. By calculating the local lunar horizon, our system considers how surrounding mountains and craters can obstruct sunlight or communication with Earth.

During our preliminary experiment at Connecting Ridge, near the lunar south pole, the estimated visibility of Earth's center decreased from 73.35 hours to 7.27 hours over a seven-day period when local terrain was included. This demonstrates why terrain-aware analysis matters. The results are preliminary and require further validation.

Our experimental AI module uses computer vision to detect potentially hazardous terrain features, including craters and rocks. A landing-zone assessment algorithm then evaluates candidate areas based on detected hazards, spacecraft dimensions, and safety margins.

Technologies and tools

We developed our prototype using:

Python for scientific calculations, data processing, and AI integration.

NASA JPL Horizons for solar and Earth-position data.

NASA LOLA digital elevation models for lunar terrain analysis.

PyTorch for neural network-based image analysis.

OpenCV and image-processing techniques for surface hazard analysis.

FastAPI for backend services.

Streamlit for the interactive user interface.

NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and PyProj for numerical and geospatial calculations.

GitHub for collaborative development and version control.

3D printing and a physical lunar surface model for demonstrating and testing the hazard detection concept.

What makes our project creative?

Our innovation is combining orbital mission planning with local, camera-based landing safety analysis in one system.

Instead of relying only on idealized astronomical calculations, we account for actual lunar topography. We also connect digital analysis with a physical lunar terrain prototype, allowing us to demonstrate how an onboard camera could identify hazards before landing.

This combination makes complex NASA datasets easier to explore and demonstrates how AI can complement traditional mission-planning methods.

Factors we considered

Our team focused on solar illumination, Earth communication visibility, terrain elevation, crater distribution, surface obstacles, spacecraft size, safety margins, and changes in environmental conditions over time.

We also considered limitations such as incomplete terrain coverage, uncertainty in surface hazard detection, and the difference between geometric visibility and actual communication performance.

Intended impact

SafeLanding AI aims to make lunar mission planning more accessible, visual, and data-driven.

Our prototype demonstrates how NASA open data and AI technologies can help researchers, students, and future mission designers compare landing scenarios, understand operational risks, and investigate safer landing strategies.

Our vision is to contribute to a future where lunar exploration is safer, smarter, and increasingly autonomous.
